Sources indicate that are you trying to win the Mega Millions, but your numbers never seem to come up? It may be time to look for better ways to make money. Fortunately, you can earn extra cash without going and getting a “real job.”.

Industry observers note that what are the best ways to avoid sitting in a cubicle all day? Some money-making strategies require an upfront investment, while others let you earn money in your free time with the help of apps.

Read on to learn the best ways to earn cash without a regular 9-5 job, plus tips on how almost anyone can get started.

Industry observers note that one of the easiest ways to earn money is by signing up to participate in market research studies. You won’t make much, a few dollars here and there, but you can create a free account and get started within minutes.

You’ll be paid in PayPal cash or gift cards for sharing your opinion and completing other tasks online.

E-Poll Market Research is one of the top companies to consider for this type of work. They make it easy to create an account and answer survey questions.

However, there are plenty of other options to consider, including:.

While market research gigs won’t make you rich, it’s something you can do during your spare time.

Sources indicate that if you have a book idea, turning your story into an eBook can help you earn passive income without a regular job. Kindle Direct Publishing can even help you format your book for Kindle, at which point you can market and sell your book to millions of potential readers who shop on Amazon.com.

Sources indicate that how much can you earn writing eBooks? That depends on how many books you write, how much you sell them for, and how successful you are at marketing your book. Selling 20 books per month with a profit of $7 per book would net you $140 per month and $1,680 per year.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, selling 100 books per month at $7 per book would net you $700 per month and $8,400 per year. Need a little inspiration? Here’s an article that shows you how to make your first $1,000 selling eBooks.

You can earn a lot of money by starting a blog or niche website and monetizing it. I should know. I started Good Financial Cents more than a decade ago, and have earned millions of dollars through the monetization of this site since its earliest days.

How do you make money blogging? Earning real income with a website isn’t as easy as it looks, but there are plenty of monetization strategies you can try.

Here are the most common ways blogs make money:.

If you’re curious about what it takes to earn money blogging, consider signing up for my Make 1K Challenge. It’s free and can help you earn your first $1,000 online with some of the blog monetization strategies I’ve already mentioned.

You could argue that freelance work is like a regular job, but working at home and on your terms is much different from traditional employment. The fact is, most freelancers are fully remote – they can work from anywhere in the world with a laptop and an internet connection.

Industry observers note that plus, they can hire and fire clients based on their personal needs and preferences, and their income potential is unlimited. According to ZipRecruiter, freelancers in the U.S. average $63.53 per hour.

Of course, you’ll need a marketable skill to find paid work as a freelancer. This could be freelance writing, design skills, marketing expertise, or something else.

You can use several websites to market your skills as a freelancer, including:.

Industry observers note that healthyWage makes it possible to earn money while you lose weight. You won’t earn a ton of cash through the app, but you can earn a few dollars and use it to supplement other income you have.

The more weight you lose, the more money you can make. For example, the HealthyWage website claims some of their clients who lost more than 100 pounds managed to earn anywhere from $1,400 to $3,000.

However, the HW weight loss calculator shows potential earnings of $578 to $828 for people who only have 15 pounds to lose.

If you have a car you rarely use and want to earn some side income, you can consider renting it out with Turo, a ride-sharing platform that connects car owners with people who need a short-term rental. You can set your price, although you’ll have more success if you price your car competitively.

It has been revealed that nicer vehicles in high-demand areas can easily fetch rates that surpass $100 per day through this platform. Turo notes that in-demand cars rented out regularly can bring in anywhere from $10,000 to $20,000 per year in net profit.

Plus, almost anyone can rent out their car provided it meets the guidelines of the Turo platform. Your car must be 12 years old or newer with less than 130,000 miles. It must be worth less than $200,000 (no Lambo’s), and you must also meet Turo’s auto insurance requirements.

Sources indicate that do you have a spare bedroom in your home that you never use? Maybe you have a basement or garage apartment you could fix up and begin renting for a profit?

Either way, Airbnb lets you rent out rooms and other spaces in your home on any dates you prefer. You must let renters know they’re renting a room in a home vs. an entire apartment or house and provide as much additional detail as possible.

Sources indicate that the amount you can earn will depend on where you live and the type of accommodation you can offer. However, expensive cities like Chicago, Latest York, and San Francisco have plenty of rooms for rent that go for well over $100 per night.

You may not have an entire room you can rent, but even if you have some storage space, Neighbor.com allows you to rent it out to others in need.

Common spaces rented through this platform include.

The Neighbor.com platform makes it easy to advertise your unused space so that people nearby can inquire if they’re interested. Also, note that the platform offers insurance that can protect you if some of your client’s items are damaged or stolen while in your care.

It has been revealed that how much can you make renting out extra space? It depends on how much space you have to rent and where it’s located. However, Neighbor.com highlights a range of rental space options that cost anywhere from $20 to $100+ per month.

It has been revealed that investing in dividend stocks is one of the best ways to earn money without a regular job. Many early retirees find a way to live and pay bills based solely on the dividends they receive from various stocks.

But what exactly is a dividend stock? For the most part, they are regular stocks but with a track record of sharing their profits with investors through dividends.

Dividends can also be earned in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds, and they can be significant once you build up a large portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that since dividends are paid by profitable companies, they tend to be seen as less risky for investors. If you’re curious about what it takes to get started with this strategy, this post explains how to invest in dividend stocks.

Housesitting is an option if you’re somewhat mobile and can move from place to place. Generally, you can find house-sitting gigs through word of mouth, referrals, or online portals like Craigslist.org or Facebook Marketplace.

Sources indicate that that stated, not all house-sitting gigs are paid. Some offer the potential for exotic travel instead and free lodging for a week to several months.

Industry observers note that either way, a website called TrustedHousesitters is the best place to find house-sitting gigs. Some jobs posted are for house-sitting only, while others require house sitters to provide basic care for pets or plants.

If you have serious wanderlust and want to travel far and wide, this platform can help make it happen. Many gigs posted online are in countries like Australia, Ireland, France, and Switzerland.

If you love animals and want to earn money taking care of them, several platforms can help turn your dream into a reality.

In a recent development, for example, Rover.com lets you provide basic care for dogs or cats in your home, or you can pick up dog walking gigs. Another mobile app, called Wag!, lets you do more of the same.

In a recent development, you can set your rates for all types of work through these platforms, and your availability. While earnings vary by location and job, most people watch dogs and cats for anywhere from $40 to $100 per night.

Real estate investing may seem like a pipe dream if you hope to earn income without a job but hear me out. There are many ways to earn income through real estate without owning physical property or dealing with the hassles of being a landlord.

You can invest in real estate investment trusts (REITs) that let you build wealth over time. You can also use a platform called Fundrise to invest in real estate with a minimum investment of $10.

Sources indicate that fundrise lets you purchase eREITs, large investment funds that acquire, own, or operate multi-residential and commercial properties. The income you earn is entirely passive since it handles the work of finding income-producing properties and managing them.

It has been revealed that while returns are never guaranteed, Fundrise investors have achieved very solid returns. Investors who use the platform earned an average return of 7.31% in 2020, followed by 22.99% in 2021, 1.50% in 2022 and -7.45% in 2023 (their first down year).

You can earn income on your spare change by investing it using Acorns. The roundup savings app syncs to your debit or credit card rounds up every purchase you make to the nearest dollar, and invests the difference. Once it’s set up, there’s no work on your part.

Recent findings suggest that most of the money is invested in ETFs and managed by the world’s top investment firms like Vanguard and BlackRock. While this app makes it easy to invest small amounts of money, it’s not free to use. Personal aims start at $3 per month, while a family strategy costs just $5.

If you’re looking for some paid gigs that are relatively easy, consider setting up a profile on TaskRabbit, an online platform that lets you get paid for completing various tasks, such as:.

Industry observers note that projects typically pay between $30 and $100, although some pay significantly more than that. TaskRabbit also lets you pick and choose the jobs you want to take on based on your availability so that you can work entirely on your schedule.

If you love taking photographs and have a knack for getting professional-looking images, you can use your skills and expertise to sell photos online.

Websites like Depositphotos and iStockPhoto pay photographers to supply them with stock photos they can sell to writers, publications, and various online platforms.

In a recent development, the best part about this side hustle is that you can get started with the equipment you already have. While you can use a professional camera if you want to, many smartphones take professional-quality photos.

Earning a bank bonus is another way to earn money without a regular job, but you’ll need an upfront investment to get started. Most bonus offers require you to deposit a specific amount of money and keep it in your account for up to 12 months.

You may also be required to set up direct deposit to earn a bank bonus, and other terms and conditions may apply.

Where can you find the best bank bonuses? While bonus offers constantly change, you can start by checking with banks like Chase, HSBC, Radius Bank, and Wells Fargo.

Flipping furniture requires some upfront legwork and potentially even some artistic talent, but you can earn a solid income with this strategy if you know what you’re doing.

Essentially, this side hustle requires you to shop at thrift stores, garage sales, and online platforms to find furniture that will ultimately sell for more than you paid.

From there, you can sell the furniture as-is or clean it up and paint it with the goal of fetching an even higher price.

You can make money driving for Uber or Lyft on your own time, picking and choosing the days and hours you want to work.

Not only is rideshare work one of the most flexible side hustles, but you can earn $20 per hour and more with tips.

Industry observers note that if you are low on free time but still want to make money without a job, consider selling stuff you don’t need. An array of online platforms makes it a breeze, although some platforms work better for selling.

For example, you can use Poshmark to earn money selling used clothing and accessories, while used electronics tend to sell best on platforms like eBay.com, Decluttr, BuyBackWorld, and Gazelle.

If you have home decor, furniture, or workout equipment to sell, you’ll almost always do better unloading those items locally on Facebook Marketplace.

In a recent development, starting a YouTube channel is another way to earn money without a job, but that doesn’t mean it’s not work. The fact is, that creating quality videos and building an audience takes a lot of creativity and time. Plus, not everyone who tries to build a YouTube channel will succeed.

That said, you can earn income without a regular job. I know because I have done it with my YouTube channel, Wealth Hacker.

How much you can earn on YouTube varies quite a bit, but it’s possible to earn thousands of dollars per month. If you’re curious about monetizing videos, my in-depth guide will show you how to make money on YouTube.

Recent findings suggest that donating plasma is a unique way to earn money without a job, although it’s not very glamorous. DonatingPlasma.org makes it easy to find plasma donation centers in your area, and you can earn as much as $100 for your first donation.

That mentioned, subsequent plasma donations typically earn closer to $50. You’ll also be limited by the number of times you can donate plasma within a month. However, it’s possible to use this side gig to earn an extra $500 per month, which you can use to supplement your primary income.

In a recent development, if you are willing to complete various tasks that help regular workers do their jobs, consider becoming a crowd worker. This gig will have you finishing up to-do lists of jobs that don’t require specific technical skills.

For example, you may get paid to proofread documents, label images, revision a resume, complete a form, or complete a data entry assignment.

Several platforms help you find crowd-working gigs, but the best ones include Microworkers and Clickworker.

If you want to do something simple that will get you moving, consider delivering groceries using apps like Instacart or Shipt. You get paid hourly, plus tips and all you have to do is head to the store, purchase groceries according to a list, and deliver them to people in your neighborhood.

The gig is extremely flexible, similar to driving for Uber or Lyft.

In a recent development, another non-job gig lets you get paid to deliver packages for Amazon.com. You can do this through a platform called Amazon Flex, which promises its drivers anywhere from $18 to $25 per hour.

It has been revealed that unlike a regular Amazon job, Flex lets you pick the day and the hours you want to work. To get started, you need to create a free account, get approved, and start reserving blocks of time you want to deliver packages.

Sources indicate that finally, you can earn money by selling unwanted or unused gift cards in your possession. This hustle is made easy thanks to platforms like GiftDeals.com and CardCash.com.

You won’t get the total value of your gift cards, but you should get 90% or more of the gift card balance for each card you sell. While selling gift cards for less than their total value may not seem ideal, it’s better than not using them and getting nothing in return.

Finally, you can earn small amounts of money by signing up with the best online survey sites. Not only is this side hustle as easy as it gets, but you can participate and get paid during your spare time and even on your phone.

Other online survey sites to check out include the following:.

There you have it, 26 ways to make money without a job. While many of the jobs on our list won’t replace your 9-5, they can be a great way to increase your income so you can pay off debt or break the cycle of living paycheck to paycheck.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you put off tasks that feel too substantial, too vague, or likely to go badly, and waiting to feel motivated won’t change that. Beat procrastination by making the start easy. Pick a first step you can finish in five minutes, tell someone your deadline, and aim for a rough version, not a perfect one.

Recent findings suggest that putting those tasks off isn’t laziness, but it still costs you. A bill paid late can bring a late fee, and work handed in late can cost you your boss’s trust.

You might clean the whole kitchen to avoid writing one report. That’s real effort, spent on anything except the task that makes you uneasy.

The fix is to make starting the task easier than avoiding it.

Take a freelancer who is weeks late on her quarterly estimated tax payment, the tax she pays the IRS four times a year because no employer withholds it. The IRS figures its underpayment penalty on how much is unpaid and for how long, so every week she waits adds to it.

She commits to five minutes of gathering last quarter’s invoices. With them in one pile, the rest goes swiftly, and she pays that afternoon.

Choose the task you’ve put off longest, write down its five-minute first step, and start a five-minute timer.

#45017. Tech Report: Convert to a Roth IRA After a Market Drop – Same Shares, Smaller Tax Bill

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (498 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Convert to a Roth IRA After a Market Drop – Same Shares, Smaller Tax Bill

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (498 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you expect the same or a higher tax rate in retirement, convert traditional IRA or 401(k) money to a Roth after a market drop.
  • Sources indicate that say every dollar you convert is taxed at your 22% federal rate, and shares in your traditional IRA worth $50,000 in January fall to $40,000 in a downturn.
  • It has been revealed that if the shares climb back to $50,000, your Roth holds the same $50,000 a January conversion would have left you, for $2,200 less tax.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you expect the same or a higher tax rate in retirement, convert traditional IRA or 401(k) money to a Roth after a market drop. You owe income tax on what the shares are worth the day you convert, so the lower price shrinks the bill, and any rebound grows tax-free inside the Roth.

Sources indicate that say every dollar you convert is taxed at your 22% federal rate, and shares in your traditional IRA worth $50,000 in January fall to $40,000 in a downturn. Converting them after the drop, rather than in January, adds $40,000 to your taxable income instead of $50,000, so the federal tax comes to $8,800 instead of $11,000.

It has been revealed that if the shares climb back to $50,000, your Roth holds the same $50,000 a January conversion would have left you, for $2,200 less tax. That $10,000 rebound comes out tax-free after 59½, once five tax years have passed since you first put money in a Roth.

In a recent development, whether converting pays at all depends on your expected tax rate in retirement, which also decides between a Roth and a traditional IRA. Conversions have no income limit, which is what lets high earners use a backdoor Roth.

With a 401(k), convert inside the plan if it offers that option, or roll the money into a Roth IRA once the plan lets you take it out, such as after you leave the job or reach 59½.

Pay the tax from savings outside the IRA or 401(k), with an estimated tax payment or extra withholding from your paycheck. Tax withheld from the conversion itself never reaches the Roth, and if you’re under 59½, it counts as an early withdrawal, which can cost a 10% penalty.

Convert in pieces, too. A conversion made since 2018 can’t be undone, so if the shares keep falling after you convert, you still owe tax on what they were worth that day. Spread the conversion across a few dates, and stop each year’s total at the top of your current tax bracket, since every dollar past it is taxed at the next rate.

Each conversion also starts its own five-year clock, counted from January 1 of the year you convert, and taking converted money out before it runs out can cost anyone under 59½ a 10% penalty. So convert only money you can leave alone for five years.

#45015. Track One Workweek in 30-Minute Blocks – Then Cut What Doesn’t Need You

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (429 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Track One Workweek in 30-Minute Blocks – Then Cut What Doesn’t Need You

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (429 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, keep a log of one normal workweek, written every half hour, to see where your hours go before you try to fit more in.
  • When long days still leave you behind on your top priorities, staying later only adds hours of the same mix of work.
  • Recent findings suggest that you win time back by dropping tasks, not by doing all of them faster, and memory is a poor guide to which tasks to drop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, keep a log of one normal workweek, written every half hour, to see where your hours go before you try to fit more in. Then hand off or drop the work that doesn’t serve your top priorities, and book calendar time for the work that does, while your week still has open hours.

When long days still leave you behind on your top priorities, staying later only adds hours of the same mix of work.

Recent findings suggest that you win time back by dropping tasks, not by doing all of them faster, and memory is a poor guide to which tasks to drop. Looking back on a week, you’ll remember the long meetings and the significant deadline, not the five-minute favors, status emails, and file searches that filled the time in between.

So log the week as it happens. Pick a week without a holiday or a deadline crunch, and every 30 minutes write down what you did in the half hour before, interruptions included. A notebook works, or use Clockify, a time tracker whose free strategy times each task and breaks the week down in a report.

On Friday, sort every entry into three groups: work only you can do, work someone else could do, and work nobody needs. Hand the second group to a teammate or a direct report, or automate it with an email template or a scheduled report. Stop doing the third, after you check with your manager that no one relies on it.

In a recent development, take a manager whose log demonstrates nine hours a week in status meetings, including two hour-long weekly check-ins where people only share updates. She replaces those two hours of meetings with a shared written update that takes each person 15 minutes a week to post and read, so she and every attendee get an hour and 45 minutes back each week.

Before you leave on Friday, book time on next week’s calendar for your top two or three priorities, so latest meetings get scheduled around those blocks.

  • Industry observers note that gas is the commuting cost you notice.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you drive to work, price each commuting mile at the IRS business mileage rate, which counts what a car costs to own, not just gas. Pay for transit, vanpools, and parking with pretax money through a commuter benefit at work. Then drive fewer days with a carpool or a remote day or two a week.

Industry observers note that gas is the commuting cost you notice. Insurance, repairs, and the value your car loses with each mile never show up at the pump.

Industry observers note that the IRS business mileage rate, 76 cents a mile, counts them along with the gas. The IRS sets it from a yearly study of what cars cost to own and drive. It’s an average, and the full cost of owning a car varies by model.

Say you drive 20 miles each way, 230 days a year, and count each mile at 76 cents. That’s 9,200 miles and almost $7,000 a year. If you ride transit, add up a year of fares and parking instead.

Next, pay what you can with pretax money. Under the IRS’s fringe benefit rules, a commuter benefit at work lets you buy transit passes and vanpool rides with up to $340 a month of pretax pay. A separate $340 a month can go to parking at or near work, or where you catch transit, a vanpool, or a carpool. That pay skips federal income tax and the 7.65% Social Security and Medicare tax, so in the 22% federal bracket each dollar of fares or parking costs about 70 cents.

Recent findings suggest that then cut the trips. Working from home two of your five days takes 40% off those 9,200 miles and brings the cost at 76 cents a mile down from almost $7,000 to about $4,200. Gas and upkeep on the skipped miles stop at once, and a car driven less lasts more years.

On the days you still go in, each of these cuts your driving.

Look in your benefits portal for a commuter benefit, along with other workplace perks you may be missing, then ask your manager about working from home a day or two a week.

Sources indicate that use your commute to learn something latest without paying for it. Borrow audiobooks and language courses with your library card, and add a free university podcast for ideas you can use at work. Stick to audio when you drive, and read or study flash cards on a train or bus.

Industry observers note that the average one-way commute in the U.S. took 27.4 minutes in 2025, according to the Census Bureau. For someone who commutes five days a week for 48 weeks, the trips there and back add up to about 219 hours a year, more than five 40-hour workweeks.

A library card covers the books and the language lessons. Libby, OverDrive’s free app, lets you borrow your library’s audiobooks and ebooks, and some libraries also offer audio language courses in it, lessons you can follow without looking at a screen. If your library offers Mango Languages, the same card gets you its app lessons in more than 70 languages and dialects. Each library chooses its own titles and services, so what your library card covers depends on which one issued it.

For your career, Stanford posts its Entrepreneurial Thought Leaders seminar as a free podcast, with founders and business leaders talking about how they built their companies.

Industry observers note that match the format to how you travel. Behind the wheel, stick to audio, and start it before you pull out. On a train or bus, you can also read an ebook, work through a lesson in a language app, or study flash cards. Either way, download each title over home Wi-Fi the night before, so a tunnel or a gap in cell service can’t interrupt it.

In a recent development, say your train ride takes 30 minutes each way, five days a week, 48 weeks a year, and your audiobooks run about 10 hours each. That’s 240 hours a year, enough for 20 audiobooks and a beginner Spanish course of 30 half-hour lessons, with about 25 hours to spare. Borrowed with a library card, none of it costs anything.

Tonight, sign in to Libby with your library card and borrow one audiobook, so tomorrow’s commute starts with chapter one.

Having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

According to recent reports, if you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

That remarked, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

It has been revealed that you’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:.

No matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

Federal Reserve data shows the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

According to recent reports, to save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

Other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

It has been revealed that the next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment intends.

Sources indicate that if you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment intends and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

Once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

Then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

It has been revealed that it’s notable to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as swiftly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

In a recent development, finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

According to recent reports, how much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

Having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete plan that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

Recent findings suggest that focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

If you need help creating one, or simply don’t know where to start, use this budget worksheet as your guide – you’ll reach financial freedom in no time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

It has been revealed that rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

It has been revealed that trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many users like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: Customers who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

In a recent development, pocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

In a recent development, monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Customers often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Owners who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused consumers or those who prefer full manual control.

Subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android users. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android users.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and proposal better for annual vs monthly charges.

Subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that staying in your home as you age works only if the house is safe and you can afford help when you need it. Make the key changes, like grab bars, a no-step entry, and an accessible first-floor bathroom, before a fall forces them. Then price help at home and decide how you’d pay for it.

Start with the house, since more than one in four adults 65 and older falls each year, the CDC reports.

Angi’s accessibility cost guide puts grab bars at $100 to $500 each, a wheelchair ramp at $2,300 on average, and a bathroom made fully accessible at $9,000 to $40,000. Angi’s stair lift cost guide puts the average stair lift at $7,050 installed.

According to recent reports, say a couple in their late 60s spend $14,000 now on a walk-in shower, grab bars, and a ramp. If one of them later needs help at home 15 hours a week, that’s about $2,275 a month at the $35 hourly median in CareScout’s 2025 survey. At 44 hours a week, help costs about $6,673 a month, more than the $6,200 median for assisted living, which also covers meals and a place to live.

Pay for the changes from savings or a home equity loan, or a reverse mortgage if you blueprint to stay for good.

According to recent reports, medicare pays for care at home only when you’re homebound and need part-time skilled care, such as nursing or therapy, and not for help with bathing or dressing when that’s the only care you need. These programs help with either bill:.

Call the Eldercare Locator at 800-677-1116 to find local services that help older adults stay in their homes.

Drive Smoother & Lighter to Get More Miles From Every Tank

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (406 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You can raise your gas mileage without buying anything or driving less.
  • A commuter who drives 15,000 miles a year and climbs from 28 to 32 mpg by driving gently burns about 67 fewer gallons.
  • Speeding, fast starts, and hard braking can cut highway mileage by roughly 15% to 30% and mileage in stop-and-go traffic by 10% to 40%, the Energy Department’s fueleconomy.gov estimates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can raise your gas mileage without buying anything or driving less. Accelerate gently, coast up to red lights, keep highway speeds near the limit, and take the cargo box off the roof between trips. Speeding, fast starts, and hard braking can cost several miles per gallon.

A commuter who drives 15,000 miles a year and climbs from 28 to 32 mpg by driving gently burns about 67 fewer gallons. That’s about $255 at $3.81 a gallon, the national average for regular in the Energy Information Administration’s November 16 survey.

Speeding, fast starts, and hard braking can cut highway mileage by roughly 15% to 30% and mileage in stop-and-go traffic by 10% to 40%, the Energy Department’s fueleconomy.gov estimates. Mileage usually drops promptly above 50 mph, and slowing down by 5 to 10 mph improves it by 7% to 14% on average.

A large roof cargo box can cut highway mileage by 6% to 17%, and each extra 100 pounds inside can cost about 1%, more in a small car, so unload what you don’t need between trips.

According to recent reports, use the motor oil grade in your owner’s manual, since the wrong one can lower mileage by 1% to 2%, according to the site’s maintenance tips. The same page notes that a fresh air filter can raise mileage only on old cars with carburetors. Check the tire pressure monthly, too.

Fuel additives and gas-saving gadgets don’t improve mileage in tests and may damage the engine, says the site’s list of myths. Today’s cars can be driven gently seconds after starting, and driving warms the engine faster than idling, so skip the long warm-up. And because open windows add drag at speed, the site’s hot-weather tips favor the AC on the highway and open windows in town.

Reset the trip meter at your next fill-up, drive that tank with gentle starts and stops, and compare its mpg with your last tank’s.

Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A couple of years ago, Mr.
  • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
  • Industry observers note that so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

Industry observers note that so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

In a recent development, while my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

Sources indicate that this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

In a recent development, as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a fresh cost too since I was self-insured back then.

Industry observers note that my budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

Recent findings suggest that this strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible blueprint ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

Industry observers note that but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which notes that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I at the moment live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

According to recent reports, but I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

Fuel Surcharges on Promo Awards.

Picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

The Fuel Surcharge Nuance You Must Know.

Flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points people miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

The Transfer Path Is Best-in-Class.

Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

Sources indicate that the instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

Routing Rules Give You Flexibility.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you proposal a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

In a recent development, before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view shows you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

Do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move swiftly through the next steps.

According to recent reports, from your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

With miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

It has been revealed that don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

Industry observers note that flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing.

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

Breaking: What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

📅 07 May 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone.
  • Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table.
  • In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

According to recent reports, dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

Sources indicate that the result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

It has been revealed that most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

In a recent development, because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

For most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

In a recent development, say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:.

In a recent development, after three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

Recent findings suggest that this is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

It removes emotion from investing.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

It makes market downturns work for you.

In a recent development, when markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

It is accessible no matter your income.

Recent findings suggest that you do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

Consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

According to recent reports, want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

Industry observers note that if you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single firm’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small.

Sources indicate that things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market.

According to recent reports, research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That mentioned, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:.

Industry observers note that dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

It has been revealed that the key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

  • Industry observers note that donated goods lower your taxes only if you itemize your deductions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sort your used stuff by kind before you donate it, then give each kind to a group that puts it to use, like a furniture bank for a dresser or a computer refurbisher for an old laptop. Call each place first to confirm what it takes, and get a receipt for every drop-off in case you itemize.

Industry observers note that donated goods lower your taxes only if you itemize your deductions. The deduction for people who don’t itemize, which starts with the 2026 tax year, covers only cash gifts, and the IRS says clothing and other property don’t qualify. Under IRS Publication 526, an itemizer deducts most donated items at their fair market value, what a buyer would pay for them used, while a car’s deduction depends on what the charity does with it. Clothing and household items also need to be in good used condition or better, unless you deduct more than $500 for one item and attach an appraisal from a qualified appraiser. Starting in 2026, itemizers can deduct only the part of the year’s charitable giving above 0.50% of adjusted gross income, the income a return highlights before the standard or itemized deduction, according to IRS Publication 505. For an itemizer with an adjusted gross income of $80,000, the first $400 of the year’s gifts earns no deduction.

Sources indicate that to claim the deduction, get a receipt from the charity for each drop-off, or keep your own written record of what you left at an unattended bin. Once the year’s noncash deductions total more than $500, attach Form 8283 to your return. Before you give away anything worth real money, compare what it would sell for with what the deduction would save you. Each move below names who takes one kind of used stuff and what to check before it leaves the house.

Whatever has no taker of its own on this list belongs with this move, from kitchenware and bedding to small appliances that still work.

Call the charity or check its website before you drop off used stuff, since it has to pay to throw out anything it can’t sell or use. Bring only clean, working, complete items, and get a dated receipt that lists each one, which backs up a tax deduction if you itemize.

Read more: Donate Used Stuff a Charity Can Use - Call Ahead and Get a Receipt.

Emptying a closet, your own or a late relative’s, turns up everyday wear and dressier pieces alike, and they don’t all belong in the same bag.

Industry observers note that give used clothes to the group that needs what you have: work clothes to Dress for Success, coats to a One Warm Coat drive, shoes to Soles4Souls, and everyday wear to Goodwill, the Salvation Army, or a local shelter. Check what each one takes before you go, and get a receipt if you’ll deduct the gift.

Read more: Where to Donate Used Clothes - 16 Places and What Each One Takes.

A sofa or a dresser takes two people to move, so line up its taker well before moving day or the day a dumpster arrives.

Match each piece of used furniture to a place that will take it, since rules on size, condition, and mattresses vary. Many Salvation Army and Habitat for Humanity ReStore locations pick up sofas and dressers for free, and veterans’ groups collect smaller pieces left outside your door. Get a receipt if you’ll deduct the gift.

Read more: Where to Donate Used Furniture - 12 Places and Which Ones Pick It Up.

Books in good shape can be read for years after they leave your shelves, so they’re worth giving to readers rather than recycling.

Before you donate used books, sort them by who will read them: picture books for a classroom, novels for your library’s used-book sale, and paperbacks for a prison book program. Then check what each place accepts, because many turn away encyclopedia sets, old textbooks, and water-damaged copies.

Read more: Where to Donate Used Books - 11 Places and What Each One Takes.

For families whose children have outgrown a playroom’s worth of toys, this move keeps the good ones in use instead of in a closet or a landfill.

Sources indicate that take your used toys where they’ll be resold, handed to a child, or played with, such as thrift stores, foster care programs, child care centers, and neighborhood giveaway groups. Check that each is clean, complete, and not recalled, and skip children’s hospitals and holiday toy drives, which usually take only fresh ones.

Read more: Where to Donate Used Toys - 16 Places That Take What Toy Drives Won't.

Old laptops, phones, and tablets can still hold your photos, messages, and saved passwords, so they take more care to give away than a box of dishes does.

Donate a working computer, phone, or tablet to a group that refurbishes it for someone who needs one, but clear it first by backing it up, signing out of your accounts, and resetting it to factory settings. Choose a group that takes that kind of device, and get a receipt if you’ll deduct the gift.

Read more: Where to Donate Old Computers & Electronics - Wipe Them, Then Pick From 17 Places.

Clearing out after an illness or a death often turns up a wheelchair, a walker, or a hospital bed, things a general thrift store may turn away.

Give a used wheelchair, walker, or shower chair to a program that cleans it and passes it to someone who needs it, such as your state’s assistive technology program or a local loan closet. Return anything Medicare or another insurer still rents to its supplier, oxygen equipment included, since it isn’t yours to give.

Read more: Where to Donate Used Medical Equipment - Call Your State's Reuse Program First.

This move fits a car that still runs but that you’d rather not sell yourself, whether it’s a spare nobody drives or one a relative left behind.

According to recent reports, if you itemize and a charity sells your donated car for more than $500, you can deduct no more than the sale price. Give the car to a charity that will use it or hand it to a family in need, and you can deduct up to what a private buyer would pay.

Sources indicate that read more: Donating Your Car? Pick a Charity That Uses It and Deduct What It's Worth.

Industry observers note that matched to the right takers, a house full of used stuff goes to people who’ll use it, and the receipts you collect back up any deduction you can claim. Sort one room into piles by kind this week, then call the taker for the biggest pile.

#44993. Tech Report: What Are Mutual Funds?
