Tech Report: What Are Mutual Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list.
  • This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.
  • It has been revealed that A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

It has been revealed that A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

Each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

Sources indicate that when you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

Industry observers note that for example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it plans to do it.

According to recent reports, investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund organization or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

In a recent development, these funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds (fixed income funds).

According to recent reports, bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

These funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Industry observers note that index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most key things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

Sources indicate that the problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

According to recent reports, for most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

The expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Industry observers note that some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

These are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

Sources indicate that when you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

Sources indicate that for investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

In a recent development, most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly.

Industry observers note that this is the biggest problem with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Sources indicate that because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

Industry observers note that when a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an concern in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

In a recent development, it is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

Recent findings suggest that with thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

According to recent reports, mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

In a recent development, that said, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most notable step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

Tech Report: What Are Target Date Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.
  • According to recent reports, A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment.
  • According to recent reports, the fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.

According to recent reports, A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund that most closely matches the year you blueprint to retire, and the fund handles everything else. If you plan to retire around 2050, for example, you would choose a fund labeled something like “2050 Retirement Fund” or “Target Date 2050.”.

According to recent reports, the fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer. Early on, the fund is weighted heavily toward growth stocks. As retirement approaches, the portfolio gradually shifts toward bonds and more conservative holdings to reduce risk.

The appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly, and the fund adjusts itself. For people who want to set it and forget it, that sounds like a dream. But there is more to the story.

Target date funds are known as “fund of funds.” Rather than holding individual stocks or bonds directly, they hold a collection of other mutual funds, typically a mix of domestic stock, international stock, and bond funds.

Recent findings suggest that the fund manager adjusts the allocation over time according to a schedule called a glide path. When you are decades away from retirement, the fund might hold 90% stocks and 10% bonds. As you get closer to your target year, that ratio shifts until the fund is much more conservative, sometimes holding more bonds than stocks by the time you retire.

Sources indicate that the glide path is simply the schedule that determines how the fund’s asset allocation changes over time. Think of it as the fund’s long-term proposal for gradually reducing risk.

According to recent reports, different fund providers use different glide paths, and this matters more than most people realize. Some funds are more aggressive early on and pull back dramatically as retirement nears. Others maintain a higher stock allocation even into and through retirement, which some financial planners argue is actually smarter given how long retirement can last.

The important thing to understand is that the glide path is not customized for you. It is a one-size-fits-all formula based on your expected retirement year, nothing more. Your actual risk tolerance, health, spending intends, and other income sources are not factored in at all.

It has been revealed that the biggest selling point is that target date funds require almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly, and walk away. For someone who has no interest in managing their investments, that convenience is genuinely valuable.

In a recent development, because target date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds, you get broad diversification across asset classes in a single investment. You are not putting all your money into a single sector or tech giant.

In a recent development, over time, a portfolio can drift away from its intended allocation as different assets grow at different rates. Target date funds handle this automatically, which is one less thing you have to manage yourself.

Target date funds are not without their drawbacks, and for many investors, those drawbacks are significant enough to look for a better option.

In a recent development, because target date funds are funds of funds, they often carry two layers of fees: the expense ratio of the target date fund itself and the underlying expense ratios of the funds it holds. Even a seemingly small difference in fees can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a long investing career. Low-cost index funds, by comparison, often charge a fraction of what target date funds do.

The glide path in a target-date fund is designed for the average investor retiring in a given year. But your situation is not average. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income, or a much higher risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that is reflected in how the fund manages your money.

In a recent development, when you hand everything over to a target date fund, you give up control over your allocation. If the fund has a heavy position in international stocks or bonds that you would rather avoid, there is not much you can do about it while staying in the fund.

Variable quality across providers.

Not all target date funds are created equal. The same target year fund from two different providers can have very different allocations, fee structures, and underlying holdings. Without digging into the details, it is easy to end up in a fund that does not match your actual needs.

Sources indicate that this is where the comparison gets vital. A target date fund is actively managed in the sense that a team of people decides how to allocate and rebalance it over time. An index fund, on the other hand, simply tracks a market index like the S&P 500. There is no active management involved, which is exactly why the fees are so much lower.

Sources indicate that decades of research consistently show that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after fees. Target date funds are not immune to this problem. When you account for layered costs, many target-date funds trail what you would earn by simply holding a low-cost index fund over the same period.

It has been revealed that A simple alternative that many investors use is called a three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total market index fund, an international index fund, and a bond index fund. You set your own allocation based on your age and risk tolerance, rebalance once a year, and pay minimal fees. It takes about 30 minutes a year to manage.

Industry observers note that this approach gives you the same diversification as a target-date fund, with far more control and significantly lower costs. And as a general rule, the more of your return you keep rather than paying in fees, the better off you will be over time.

Target date funds are not the right choice for every investor, but there are situations where they make sense.

According to recent reports, even in these cases, it is worth checking the expense ratio. If your proposal offers a target-date fund with an expense ratio above 0.50%, consider whether there are lower-cost index fund options within the same plan.

Sources indicate that target date funds solve a real problem: they make it easy for people who do not want to think about investing to still participate in the market. That convenience has real value.

In a recent development, but for investors who are willing to learn even a little bit about how to manage their own allocation, a portfolio of low-cost index funds will almost always be the better long-term choice. The fees are lower, the control is greater, and the returns tend to be better over time.

If you are at the moment in a target date fund, that is not necessarily a problem. But it is worth understanding what you are paying and whether a simpler, lower-cost approach might serve you better. Investing at least 10% of your gross income is the priority. Where exactly that money goes is the next question worth asking.

Health Sharing vs. Traditional Health Insurance: Which Is Right for You?

📅 20 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives.
  • A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance firm.
  • Sources indicate that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing aims have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance firm. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Sources indicate that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA looks, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

In a recent development, traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace blueprint, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Sources indicate that solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health blueprint with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace plans are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

Industry observers note that but that gap exists because health sharing plans aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

It works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

According to recent reports, health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

According to recent reports, is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing plan and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing initiative cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.
  • In a recent development, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years.
  • This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

In a recent development, the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Recent findings suggest that is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

“The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

Sources indicate that to answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

Industry observers note that when you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

Sources indicate that if the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Industry observers note that your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

Industry observers note that but if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

But in that same time period, your share of tech giant earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

It has been revealed that so as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

That doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

But Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a massive Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

In a recent development, but what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more swiftly?

Recent findings suggest that in the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 major companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

According to recent reports, there’s one common theme in the significant tech company boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

Industry observers note that but that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a newly introduced era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

According to recent reports, they may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

Industry observers note that but the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

Industry observers note that while the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

It has been revealed that as I said earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

Everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

It has been revealed that wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

Just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

Industry observers note that so far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

What About Paying Off Your House?

According to recent reports, over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.

Sources indicate that picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

Sources indicate that when Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

It has been revealed that on a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

According to recent reports, the routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

According to recent reports, the best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:.

In a recent development, chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear quickly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

Sources indicate that booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Industry observers note that start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

This is the most key and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:.

Sources indicate that complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

Sources indicate that A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

In Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Carpool with a coworker or neighbor who lives along your route, and take turns driving to work. Driving every other day halves what each of you spends on gas, upkeep, and tolls, and even two shared days of a five-day week cut your commuting miles by a fifth.

Sources indicate that each commuting mile you don’t drive saves more than the gas it would burn. For an average new car, AAA’s 2026 Your Driving Costs study puts fuel at 17 cents a mile and maintenance, repairs, and tires at 12 cents, with gas averaging $4.15 a gallon.

That’s about 29 cents a mile in all, well under the IRS’s mileage rate for business driving, which also counts fixed costs you keep paying however little you drive. Say you and a coworker who lives nearby both drive 25 miles to work, five days a week, 50 weeks a year. Take turns every day and each of you skips 6,250 miles a year, worth about $1,800 before any savings on parking or tolls. Take turns on just two days a week and you each still skip 2,500 miles, about $725.

Industry observers note that A second person in the car also lets you use HOV lanes, the carpool lanes for cars with two or more people, or three on some roads. Some express toll lanes charge carpools less or nothing at all.

Ask HR whether your employer runs a carpool program. Most state transportation departments and local agencies sponsor programs to help commuters share rides, from ride-matching services to vanpools, according to the Federal Highway Administration. In a vanpool, five or more riders split one monthly fare for the van and gas, which some agencies and employers subsidize. Your employer may also let you pay vanpool fares with pretax money, one of several ways to spend less on your commute.

Before the first ride, agree on who drives which days, how you’ll split gas, tolls, and parking, and what happens when someone is sick or works late. Then call your insurer to confirm your policy covers the carpool. The Texas Department of Insurance warns that regularly charging riders a fee likely won’t be covered, so split the actual costs instead.

Propose two shared days a week to the coworker who lives closest to you, or register with your area’s ride-matching program to find someone on your route.

Industry observers note that health care kept adding jobs throughout the recession, and the BLS study found the biggest gains in outpatient care, led by home health services. People still get sick and grow older in a downturn.

Utility employment rose 0.6% during the recession while total employment fell 5.4%. Homes and businesses use power and water in any economy, and someone has to keep both running.

In a recent development, government employment grew 0.8% during the recession, and most public safety workers are on government payrolls. Local governments did start trimming staff after September 2008 to cover budget shortfalls, so a long downturn can slow hiring.

A steady field lowers your risk without removing it. Public safety and teaching jobs depend on budgets that shrink in a long downturn, and a household’s other paycheck can stop, as it did for the nurse’s spouse.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Municipal bonds are loans to states, cities, and public agencies.
  • In a recent development, munis usually pay less interest than comparable taxable bonds, so the exemption pays off only if your tax bracket is high enough to make up the difference.
  • Interest on some private activity bonds, issued for private borrowers, counts toward the alternative minimum tax, a second tax calculation that can raise a higher earner’s bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Municipal bonds are loans to states, cities, and public agencies. Their interest is usually exempt from federal income tax, and often from your state’s tax when the bonds come from your own state. Hold them in a taxable brokerage account, through a low-cost muni fund rather than one bond at a time.

In a recent development, munis usually pay less interest than comparable taxable bonds, so the exemption pays off only if your tax bracket is high enough to make up the difference. Inside an IRA or 401(k), where interest isn’t taxed as it’s earned, the exemption does nothing for you.

The exemption also has limits. Interest on some private activity bonds, issued for private borrowers, counts toward the alternative minimum tax, a second tax calculation that can raise a higher earner’s bill. The gain on a bond bought below face value is taxed at your regular income rate unless the discount is tiny. And muni interest still counts in the income that sets how much of your Social Security is taxed and whether you pay higher Medicare premiums.

Sources indicate that munis come in two main kinds. General obligation bonds are backed by the issuer’s power to tax, while revenue bonds are repaid from one project’s income, such as a toll road, hospital, or water utility. Defaults are rare, especially on general obligation bonds, but Detroit’s 2013 bankruptcy and Puerto Rico’s 2017 filing to restructure its debt show they happen. A fund that holds bonds from many issuers limits what any one default can cost you.

In a recent development, individual bonds take more work. They come from a broker, usually in $5,000 pieces, with the broker’s charge, called a markup, built into the price. Before you buy one, look it up on EMMA, the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board’s free site. It demonstrates recent trade prices to compare with yours, the bond’s credit rating, and whether the issuer can call it, or repay it early.

It has been revealed that for most investors, a low-cost fund is the easier way to own munis. A national fund holds bonds from many states. A single-state fund holds only your state’s bonds, which adds the state exemption but concentrates your money there.

Choose a single-state fund only if your state’s income tax is high, as in California or Newly introduced York. Everywhere else, buy a national fund.

Even Small Gifts to Charity Lift Your Mood – and Cut Taxes Without Itemizing

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (486 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Research finds spending on others makes people happier than spending on themselves, and starting in 2026, you can deduct some cash gifts even if you take the standard deduction.
  • A tight budget is no reason to put off giving, because even a small gift can lift your mood.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a 2008 study published in Science, Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin, and Michael Norton gave people $5 or $20 to spend by 5 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giving to charity pays you back. Research finds spending on others makes people happier than spending on themselves, and starting in 2026, you can deduct some cash gifts even if you take the standard deduction. Give a set amount to a charity whose work you can see, and keep every receipt.

A tight budget is no reason to put off giving, because even a small gift can lift your mood.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2008 study published in Science, Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin, and Michael Norton gave people $5 or $20 to spend by 5 p.m. Those told to buy someone else a gift or give the money to charity were happier that evening than those told to spend it on themselves. The authors concluded that as little as $5 may be enough for a real boost in happiness that day.

It helps to see what your money does. In a 2013 follow-up study by Aknin, Dunn, Norton, and two colleagues, giving more made people happier only when the charity explained how the money would help someone, such as $10 buying a child a bed net.

The tax payoff is new. Starting in 2026, you can deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts to eligible charities, or $2,000 on a joint return, without itemizing (listing your deductions one by one). Say a married couple who file jointly, don’t itemize, and are in the 12% tax bracket give $2,000 to their local food bank. They can deduct the whole gift, which cuts their federal income tax by $240.

Industry observers note that if you do itemize, you can still deduct gifts, but only the amount above 0.50% of your adjusted gross income, your total income minus certain adjustments. Either way, only gifts to qualified charities count, and the IRS’s Tax Exempt Organization Search shows whether a charity can receive tax-deductible gifts. Money given straight to a friend for medical bills can lift your mood too, but it isn’t deductible.

For every gift, keep a bank record or a written receipt from the charity showing its name, the date, and the amount. A single gift of $250 or more also needs a written acknowledgment from the charity that notes whether you got anything in return.

Pick a charity whose work you can see, set up a monthly gift from your checking account, and keep the bank statements that show each payment.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like latest credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most vital problems for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Recent findings suggest that generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Industry observers note that most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

Industry observers note that one step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you strategy to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

According to recent reports, in fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

It has been revealed that your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That stated, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit rapidly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

In a recent development, while secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

It has been revealed that many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

It has been revealed that in fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

According to recent reports, there are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Recent findings suggest that of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an matter with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

According to recent reports, college students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

It has been revealed that either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

According to recent reports, the most affordable cities aren’t simply the cheapest but the ones where homes and rent cost the least relative to local pay. Among large U.S. metros, that’s mostly the Midwest and South, led by Akron, Ohio, and Wichita, Kansas. Before you move, check what your own job pays there, not just what houses cost.

A typical single-family home in Jackson, Mississippi, sold for $276,400 in the third quarter of 2026, less than one in Dayton, Ohio, at $281,300. Yet the Jackson home costs as much as 4.5 years of the area’s median household income, while the Dayton home costs 3.7 years’ worth, because Dayton households earn more.

Sources indicate that nationally, the typical single-family home sold for $432,900 that quarter, 5.1 years of the $84,780 median household income, and median rent took 22% of that income. In every metro below, a typical home costs less than four years of local income, and rent takes less than a fifth of it.

We started with the 104 metro areas of 500,000 or more people for which the National Association of Realtors reports home prices. For each, we compared NAR’s median price for a single-family home sold in the third quarter of 2026, and the median rent, utilities included, with median household income. The rent and income figures come from the Census Bureau’s American Community Survey for 2025.

We ranked each metro on how many years of income a typical home costs and on the share of income a typical rent takes, then added the two ranks. Ties go to the lower home price relative to income. The 15 below have the best totals among the 61 metros where overall prices run below the national average, as measured by the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s regional price parities for 2024.

Each entry gives the metro’s typical home price, rent, and household income, then a major employer and the catch.

It has been revealed that A metro’s median income indicates little about your own paycheck. Look up your occupation in the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ metro wage estimates and compare that pay with what you earn now. Then price the house you’d actually buy, with its county’s property tax and a home insurance quote, since median tax bills on this list run from $1,433 in Huntsville to $4,657 in Omaha.

The savings are biggest when you keep your current pay. Say a couple both keep remote jobs. Selling a typical home in the Washington, D.C., area, at $656,200 in the third quarter, and buying one in Harrisburg at $310,700 leaves them $345,500, minus selling and moving costs.

In a recent development, renters should compare rent with what renters there earn, since their median income runs well below the household median, $57,048 nationally against $84,780 for all households. And visit in more than one season, since climate, schools, and commutes matter too in deciding where to live.

Line up the job, or your employer’s written approval to work from the upcoming city, before you sign a lease or list your house.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, energy, and upkeep all rise with a home’s size, every year you own it.
  • Industry observers note that A bigger house is easy to justify with holiday guests or a someday you haven’t planned for.
  • Take two houses, 2,400 and 3,200 square feet, with the bigger one priced $80,000 higher.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, energy, and upkeep all rise with a home’s size, every year you own it. Size your next home for the rooms you use each week, not for holiday guests, and if you already own more space than you use, add up what those empty rooms cost you.

Industry observers note that A bigger house is easy to justify with holiday guests or a someday you haven’t planned for. Its extra rooms cost money all year, whether anyone sleeps in them or not.

Take two houses, 2,400 and 3,200 square feet, with the bigger one priced $80,000 higher. Say you borrow the difference at 7%, pay property tax at 1% of the home’s value, and set aside another 1% for upkeep, the low end of Fannie Mae’s rule of thumb of 1% to 4% a year. Put insurance at the $4.90 per $1,000 of home value that Freddie Mac’s average borrower paid in 2023.

It has been revealed that the bigger house then adds about $5,600 in first-year interest, $800 in property tax, $800 in upkeep, and $400 in insurance. Heating, cooling, and powering the extra 800 square feet add a few hundred dollars more, by our math on the Energy Information Administration’s figures for household energy spending by home size. Together, that’s close to $8,000 a year for two spare bedrooms you’d use about two weeks a year, before the furniture to fill them.

If you already own more house than you use, run the same numbers on your empty rooms. Whether selling pays is a separate calculation, since agent fees, moving costs, and the rate on a new mortgage can eat into the savings.

For your next home, blueprint for changes you can see coming, like a baby on the way or a job going remote, and favor rooms that do two jobs, such as a guest room that doubles as an office.

In a recent development, put holiday guests up in a nearby hotel instead. At about $160 a night, CoStar’s 2025 U.S. average, two hotel rooms for those two weeks cost about $4,500, against close to $8,000 a year for the spare bedrooms. Your guests sleep down the road instead of down the hall, and you keep more than $3,000 a year.

Before you tour, count the bedrooms your household used last week, and set your listing search to that number plus one flexible room.
